summary: Documents existing usage of a DHCPv4 option for the address of a TFTP server, in common use before it was officially assigned. It is defined for IPv4 addresses only and is consistent with RFC 3942. It is informational.

eli5.summary: It writes down the existing sticker that tells a new device where to fetch its starter files.

questions: what is dhcp option 150 used for
how does a voip phone find its configuration server
why avoid dns during device boot
subtitle: DHCP option 150 lets devices discover TFTP servers without DNS.

tldr.problem: VoIP and other devices need to find configuration servers, but the standard DHCP methods either require DNS lookups or only pass hostnames, adding unnecessary complexity and failure points.
tldr.mechanism: DHCP option 150 carries one or more IPv4 addresses of TFTP configuration servers directly, allowing devices to use them immediately without DNS resolution.
tldr.outcome: Devices can bootstrap with minimal firmware complexity and without depending on DNS infrastructure, making configuration more reliable and boot times faster.

today: RFC 5859 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. Option 150 continues to be used in production networks for configuring VoIP devices and other equipment that needs to discover TFTP servers without DNS.

sections.title: The Bootstrap Problem
sections.content:
Voice over IP devices like IP phones need to download their configuration from a server on the network when they first start up. The DHCP protocol can tell a device about a TFTP server in two ways: through the sname field in the DHCP header or through the TFTP Server Name option (option 66). Both of these deliver only a hostname, and the device must then look up that hostname with DNS to get an IP address.

This creates a problem for minimal devices: they must implement the DNS protocol in their firmware, consuming memory and processing power. It also introduces a point of failure: if DNS is down, the device cannot boot and contact its configuration server, even though the device is connected to the network.
sections.eli5: Old methods give a phone a server's name on a piece of paper. The phone then has to look it up in a phone book (DNS), but if the phone book is missing, it cannot start up.

sections.title: Option 150: Direct Server Address
sections.content:
The TFTP Server Address option (option 150), also called the VoIP Configuration Server Address option, solves this by allowing the DHCP server to return one or more IPv4 addresses directly. The device can use these addresses immediately without any additional lookup.

Option 150 arose from practical need: some networks had already used this option in production before it was officially assigned. RFC 5859 documents this existing practice and formalizes it. The option minimum length is 4 octets (one IPv4 address), and the length field must be a multiple of 4 (so 4, 8, 12 octets, etc.), with each 4 octets representing one server address.
sections.eli5: Instead of a name, the DHCP server tells the device the actual address, like writing down 192.0.2.1 instead of company-server.

sections.title: How Devices Use the Option
sections.content:
Only the DHCP server provides option 150; the client does not send it. If a client wants this information, it requests it by including 150 in the DHCP Parameter List option (option 55).

Servers SHOULD list addresses in order of preference. Clients SHOULD use the addresses sequentially, but may also be configured to try them in random order. A device may ignore extra addresses if it can only handle a limited number (for example, it might only accept the first two addresses even if four are provided).

Each address should be tried up to four times with a 4-second wait before moving to the next address. When option 150 appears alongside option 66 (TFTP Server Name), option 150 SHOULD take priority since it provides an address immediately.
sections.eli5: The device tries the first address several times. If that one does not work, it tries the next one, like calling the first backup number if the main one is busy.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
A rogue DHCP server could use option 150 to send a device to the wrong configuration server, just as it could abuse other DHCP options specifying servers. This threat is not unique to option 150.

DHCP authentication (as defined in RFC 3118) can protect the DHCP message itself, but even authenticated DHCP does not protect the subsequent download from the TFTP server. TFTP provides no authentication or access control, so configuration files should be signed or encrypted by the client device. The full scope of securing configuration delivery is beyond this RFC.
sections.eli5: Someone could trick a phone into downloading from the wrong place. You can sign or encrypt the configuration files to make sure they are real.

sections.title: IPv4 Only
sections.content: Option 150 is defined for DHCPv4 and carries only IPv4 addresses. There is currently no defined IPv6 DHCP equivalent.
sections.eli5: This option works for the older address system (IPv4), not the newer one (IPv6).
